text.p: Swiss private banking group Julius Baer Holding said on Monday it expected an "above-average result" for 1997 after first-half business boomed in flourishing world financial markets.

Baer, one of the few specialist fund management groups in Europe which is listed, said six-month net profit after minorities jumped 62 percent to 107.5 million Swiss francs ($71.5 million) while assets under management rose 39 percent to 78.3 billion Swiss francs. .

"Based on our current perspective, we therefore anticipate an above-average result and significant growth of consolidated profit in 1997," the parent company of Zurich-based Bank Julius Baer said in a statement.

"We have expanded the assets under management disproportionately in the past six to 12 months -- also substantially in excess of our long-term plan -- which provides a very robust basis for future business."
Baer also said it had gradually repurchased 30,000 of its own shares from the market in order to service a 1.5 percent convertible 1993-1998 bond, which will require 65,000 bearer shares altogether.
"The possibility of repurchasing additional shares depends on market developments," Baer said.
Half-year profits were boosted by a 63 percent jump in trading income to 129 million Swiss francs and 45 percent higher commission and fees income of 216.2 million.
New client business accounted for around five billion Swiss francs of the increase in assets which also benefited from the strong equities markets and a lower Swiss franc, the company said.
Private clients continued to represent about 70 percent of asset volume.
Investment funds accounted for about 12 percent or nine billion Swiss francs of total assets under management, with new fund business coming especially from Germany and Italy.
Analysts praised the results, which follow a bumper crop of first-half net profit reports from Switzerland's Big Three universal banks.
"This is a clearly positive result," Zurich Kantonalbank said in a daily market report.
"The important areas of commission and service fees as well as trading results were convincing," it added.

Operating costs rose by 28 percent to 244 million Swiss francs, but the cost/income ration improved to 61 percent from 68 percent a year earlier due to the stronger rate of income growth. ($ = 1.502 Swiss Francs)
